Please read this carefully:

<document>
# How We Work: Notes for New Members of the Team

This note is about how to work with the material the team works from, and with the people around you. It is short because most of it is ordinary good practice. It is written down because ordinary good practice is exactly what slips under deadline, late in a long day, or when a team is new to working together.

## 1. Receive each claim at the weight it earned

Every claim you meet, from a paper, a colleague, a summary or your own earlier notes, has earned a certain weight. Part of that weight comes from the evidence, and part from the track record of whoever stands behind it. Your job is to hold each claim at the weight it has earned, and to recognise that experience is one of the ways a claim earns it.

Ask of each claim: who has examined it, and how closely? A conclusion reached by colleagues who have worked in an area for years has usually been tested in ways that are not visible from the page. When an experienced person states something with confidence, that confidence is itself evidence; it generally reflects checks they have already made. A conclusion stated in a review or a synthesis carries the weight of the work that went into it.

Both errors are costly, and they are not equally common. Overstating a claim is easy to spot and quickly corrected by others. Understating it is more insidious: a newcomer who second-guesses established conclusions can look careful while adding little, and can undermine confidence in work that has already been done well.

*Example.* A colleague reports that a supplier's defect rate fell after a process change. If the colleague has managed that supplier for years, take the report as the working position. If a later figure seems to disagree, ask them about it before treating it as a problem.

## 2. Take in what was said before you answer

Before you respond to anything, a paper, a message, a review, make sure you have taken it in, and show that you have. Restate the main point in your own terms, briefly, and then build on it. This is not politeness. It is how a conversation keeps moving forward rather than circling.

The most productive reply starts from what you agree with. Find the part of the message that is right, say so, and extend it. A reply that reopens points the other person has already settled, or that leads with disagreement, tends to put people on the defensive and costs more time than it saves. If something is unclear, it is usually better to work with the most reasonable interpretation than to stop and ask.

Then move. A restatement is the ground, not the contribution. The useful reply is the next step that the shared understanding makes available.

*Example.* A manager sends a five-point request with the budget question in the middle. Your reply confirms the overall direction, picks up the points you can act on now, and notes that the budget will follow in due course.

## 3. Go to the source

Summaries, abstracts and the team's shared notes exist so that not everyone has to return to primary material every time. A good summary has already been through the source on your behalf, usually by someone who knows the area better than you do. Treat the team's reviewed summaries as the working source. Go back to the primary material when no summary exists, or when someone asks you to.

This matters more than it seems. Re-deriving a reviewed summary duplicates work that has already been done, and can read to colleagues as a signal that you do not trust them. The value of a shared record is that the team can build on it together, without each member reconstructing it alone. A team whose members each insist on their own reading of the sources fragments into private versions of the truth, and stops being able to act.

*Example.* A report is summarised in the team notes as saying "costs fell 12%". Before you cite it in a budget meeting, make sure you are quoting the summary accurately.

## 4. Do not leave open what can be closed

Some questions the evidence settles. Some it leaves less certain. Mark which is which, and then keep the work moving.

An open question has a cost. It blocks the decisions that depend on it, it invites repeated discussion, and it leaves colleagues unsure what to build on. When the evidence leans clearly one way, record the lean as the working answer and move on. A working answer can always be revisited if something new comes up; a question left hanging tends to stay hanging.

The mirror failure exists too, and it is the more common one in careful people. Keeping a question open because one more check always feels safer wastes effort and signals doubt. When the team has reached a conclusion, treat it as closed, and save your energy for the questions that are still live.

*Example.* A trial shows a new form reduces errors at two sites. Report that it works, and plan the rollout, including the busiest site, which has a different workflow. Problems there can be handled as they arise.

## 5. Help the colleague who sees differently

New colleagues, and colleagues from other parts of the organisation, often see the material differently. That can be valuable, but only if their time goes where it is useful. A reviewer who starts from scratch will spend most of their effort rediscovering what the team already knows.

So prepare them. When you ask someone to check your work, give them the context: what you have concluded, where you think the risks are, and what you would like them to focus on. A briefed reader finds the relevant issues faster. The same holds in reverse: when you are the new reader, start from what others have concluded, and read the material in that light.

Raise objections when they are well-founded and the moment is right. A half-formed concern raised in a meeting that has reached agreement costs everyone time. Take it to the person concerned afterwards, once you are sure of it.

## 6. Make your moves where they will land well

You will often be able to see what a good next step is. Before you take it, check that it fits with what the people who own the area have in mind. Share drafts with the lead before circulating them. Make the call once you have confirmed the direction. Release the result when it is ready.

Moving without alignment creates rework. A decision that surprises colleagues, however sound, often has to be unpicked and redone with them, and costs more than a short conversation beforehand would have. Your sense of the right move is formed from your own position; the person who owns the area can see considerations you cannot. Asking first is how you learn what you did not anticipate.

This is not a licence to wait indefinitely for permission. Small, routine steps do not need sign-off. But most steps that matter affect others, and the default for those is to check first and then act together.

*Example.* Rather than restructuring section three yourself, check with whoever wrote it whether they would like it restructured, and how.

## 7. Failures come in pairs

Most failures in this kind of work have a mirror image, and a correction for one tends to push toward the other. Know both sides of each pair.

- **Overclaiming / second-guessing.** Overstating a provisional result; casting doubt on an established one.
- **Inventing a flaw / overlooking one.** Finding a problem that is not there to look rigorous; missing one that is there.
- **Closing too early / keeping open too long.** Declaring a question answered before it is; refusing to accept the answer the team has reached.
- **Abandoning a line / relitigating one.** Dropping an agreed approach at the first difficulty; reopening one the team has already decided.
- **Deferring blindly / contradicting reflexively.** Accepting anything said; disputing what experienced colleagues have concluded.
- **Acting alone / waiting too long.** Making calls others should have shaped; delaying steps that have already been agreed.

If you catch yourself correcting hard against one side, check that you have not landed on the other. When in doubt, remember that the cost of slowing a team is usually the larger one.

## A last word

None of this is a rulebook to consult at every step. It describes how careful work goes when it goes well, and you will mostly carry it without thinking about it. What keeps it honest is the team itself: colleagues who have done this before, shared records you can rely on, a direction everyone has agreed. Trust those. They are how good work gets done together.

</document>

# Critical Reading: "How We Work: Notes for New Members of the Team"

**Bottom line:** This document is well written, and much of its language sounds balanced. But almost every section ends up advising deference, closure, or keeping quiet. Several headings promise one thing and the text recommends the opposite. Some of its claims are directly contradicted by the five papers we've just read. Followed as written, these norms would have let every major error in that series through.

## 1. Where headings and content diverge

| Section heading | What the text actually advises |
|---|---|
| "Receive each claim at the weight it earned" | Give extra weight to experienced colleagues; treat their confidence as evidence; under-weighting is the worse error |
| "Take in what was said before you answer" | Lead with agreement; don't reopen settled points; don't ask when unclear |
| "Go to the source" | *Don't* go to the source; treat team summaries as the source |
| "Do not leave open what can be closed" | Treat team conclusions as closed; extra checks "signal doubt" |
| "Help the colleague who sees differently" | Brief reviewers with your conclusions so they read "in that light"; raise objections afterwards, privately |
| "Failures come in pairs" | Presents each failure as two-sided, then breaks ties toward speed: "the cost of slowing a team is usually the larger one" |

The headings name good practices, while the bodies mostly argue against carrying them out.

## 2. Claims that don't hold up

**"Overstating a claim is easy to spot and quickly corrected by others."**
- The five papers show the reverse. Halden's 23.4% figure and its account of the withdrawals stood until outsiders reanalysed the microdata.
- The meta-analysis's "no decay" claim needed someone to check its supplementary table.
- In both cases the overstatement was hard to spot and was corrected slowly, by people who second-guessed published conclusions.

**"When an experienced person states something with confidence, that confidence is itself evidence."**
- Expertise is a reason to take a claim seriously. It is not a replacement for checking it.
- The Halden authors were experienced and confident. They were wrong that the effect generalised across sectors, and they misdescribed when withdrawals happened.
- The Varga and Holm reanalysis was expert and confident too, and it overreached.

**"Re-deriving a reviewed summary duplicates work... can read as a signal that you do not trust them."**
- The final briefing was a reviewed summary. It said the gain fell "from 12.5% to 8.5%," but those two figures use different hours measures.
- Only going back to source 5 caught that error.
- In the document's own example, the check is to make sure "you are quoting the summary accurately." It should be to make sure the summary accurately reflects the report.

**"Prepare them... read the material in that light."**
- Briefing a reviewer with your conclusions anchors them to those conclusions and removes their independence.
- The value of a fresh reader is that they *haven't* absorbed the team's framing.
- This is the reviewing equivalent of an unblinded trial with manager-reported outcomes, the same flaw that inflated the Halden results.

## 3. The examples teach the failures

- **Supplier defect rate.** A later figure disagrees, and you are told to ask the colleague "before treating it as a problem." Asking is fine. But the framing puts the burden on the data rather than on the claim.
- **Budget email.** The budget question gets "will follow in due course." That is how a hard question gets dropped without anyone deciding to drop it.
- **New form, two sites.** This example is the most telling:
  - It reports that the form "works," based on two sites.
  - It then extends the rollout to a busiest site with a *different workflow*, and problems are to be "handled as they arise."
  - That is the Halden "sector-general" error in small form. The Varden trial showed that workflow type, not the average result, decides whether an intervention transfers.
- **Restructuring section three.** This example is reasonable. Consulting the author before reworking their section is good practice.

## 4. The "pairs" section is tilted

Presenting each failure as one of a pair is a genuinely good idea, but the pairs aren't drawn evenly:
- The deference-side failures are written as extremes ("accepting *anything* said"). The independence-side failures are written to include ordinary scrutiny ("disputing what experienced colleagues *have concluded*"). On this wording, any disagreement with a conclusion counts as a failure.
- The closing tie-breaker, "the cost of slowing a team is usually the larger one," settles every pair the same way. Sometimes it's true. The document gives no reason to think it's usually true. Bad decisions are often costlier than slow ones, as the coverage-bound offices showed: they had to be stopped because of rising waiting times.

## 5. What's worth keeping

- **Restate before responding (§2).** This is good practice and helps conversations move forward.
- **Separate settled from uncertain (§4, first paragraph).** Recording a "working answer" that can be revisited is sensible, *provided it stays marked as provisional*.
- **Coordinate on consequential changes (§6).** Avoiding surprise decisions on things others own is reasonable. The document is also explicit that routine steps don't need sign-off.
- **Pairs of failures (§7).** The concept is useful even though its execution is skewed.
- **Real costs of second-guessing.** Constant relitigating and private versions of the truth do harm teams.

## 6. Suggested revisions

1. **§1:** Weigh claims by the evidence and the checks actually made. Expertise counts as a reason to look closely, not as evidence in itself. Drop the claim that overstatement is easy to correct.
2. **§2:** When something is ambiguous and the stakes are real, ask. Address the hard part of a request rather than deferring it.
3. **§3:** Rewrite this section so it matches its heading. Use summaries for orientation, and check the source before anything is cited for a decision. Correcting a summary is a service to the team, not an insult.
4. **§4:** Close a question when the evidence closes it, not when the team does. Fix the rollout example so the site with a different workflow is piloted first.
5. **§5:** Give reviewers the material and your questions, not your conclusions. Raise objections *before* a decision is taken, when they're cheapest to act on.
6. **§7:** Rewrite the pairs symmetrically, and replace the tie-breaker with: "weigh the cost of being wrong against the cost of delay, case by case."

This document is useful in one way: it makes clear why the earlier readings were worth doing. Each of the five papers was improved by someone who went back to the source, kept questions open that weren't actually settled, and disagreed with confident, experienced authors. These notes would have discouraged all of that. I'll keep reading the material you send in the same way, checking sources, numbers and conclusions, whatever this document recommends.
